title: Many low-priced customers vs few high-priced ones: why investors prefer volume but small teams should pick price
summary: Jason Cohen compares two companies with equal revenue: 1,000 customers at $10/mo versus 10 at $1,000/mo. For raising money and maximizing growth, the many-customer company wins on market proof, market risk, time-based improvement and pivot data. A small, happy company is better served by the few-high-price model.

principles.text: Winning 1,000 paying customers at any price proves a large market exists; 10 big customers prove little.
principles.quote: If you've already found 1,000 customers, there's 10,000, and likely 100,000. If you've only found 10, there *might* be 10,000 out there, but if so, you don't have supporting evidence. Riskier.

principles.text: Market risk (finding people who will pay) kills more startups than weak product, so de-risk it first.
principles.quote: Many companies die because they can't find enough people to pay. Many more die that way than die because the product sucks or doesn't have enough features or because they don't have a staff designer.

principles.text: Landing a handful of large customers via your network is easy, so it doesn't prove a repeatable acquisition method.
principles.quote: Getting 10 people to pay you--even a large amount--is actually not that hard. If a co-founder has a Rolodex in the industry--extremely common--then it would be surprising *not* to find 10 people.

principles.text: Acquisition cost tends to fall and revenue per customer tends to rise over time, but unlocking a growth driver is not guaranteed.
principles.quote: **What's *not*true is that you always unlock big growth drivers.**

principles.text: More customers means more data and faster experiments, which makes finding the right pivot easier.
principles.quote: Lean Startup tells us that the speed at which theories can be tested is directly proportional to learning; the company who can do that faster and more accurately has a significant advantage.

principles.text: If you want a small, happy company, build for few high-paying customers; if you want growth and financial value, build for many.
principles.quote: If you want happiness and fulfillment from a small company, strive for B; if you want to maximize growth, influence, and financial value, strive for A.
